title: RAW Develop Studio & 32-bit HDR Color Pipelines
subtitle: Sensor Data Decoding, Exposure Recovery, White Balance & Lens Correction

learningObjectives: Understand digital camera RAW data and the role of Develop Studio in processing a supported RAW file.
Work in a 32-bit unbounded floating point color space (RGB/32 HDR) vs standard 8-bit / 16-bit integers.
Recover clipped highlights, open shadow details, and calibrate White Balance via the Tint and Temperature sliders.
Apply automated and manual lens profile corrections (distortion, chromatic aberration, vignette removal).
standardSections.foundationalKnowledge: When a camera captures a RAW photograph, it records sensor data that must be processed before normal viewing and sharing. In Affinity, opening a supported RAW file launches the Develop Studio, a dedicated environment for RAW processing. Its current documented panels include Basic (exposure, tone curve, enhance and white balance), Lens (distortion, rotation, chromatic aberration and vignetting), Detail (noise reduction and sharpening), Tones and Masks. The exact clipping-warning shortcuts and overlay controls formerly described in this lesson were not established by the official RAW guide reviewed here and are therefore not taught as verified behavior.

stepByStepInstructions.title: Open a RAW file in Develop Studio
stepByStepInstructions.instruction: Open a supported RAW file using File > Open. Affinity automatically opens the file in Develop Studio. Inspect the Basic panel and its exposure and white-balance controls.

stepByStepInstructions.title: Correct exposure and white balance
stepByStepInstructions.instruction: In the Basic panel, adjust Exposure, Black Point, Highlights and Shadows as needed. Use White Balance controls to adjust Temperature and Tint; the picker can sample a neutral grey or white area.

stepByStepInstructions.title: Review lens and detail corrections
stepByStepInstructions.instruction: Use the Lens panel for distortion, rotation, chromatic aberration, defringing and vignetting. Use the Detail panel for noise reduction and sharpening. Control availability depends on the RAW file and current settings.

stepByStepInstructions.title: Choose the output type
stepByStepInstructions.instruction: Choose Pixel layer for a flattened developed result, RAW layer (embedded) to keep the RAW file inside the document, or RAW layer (linked) to keep the source file at its original location.

stepByStepInstructions.title: Develop into Pixel Studio
stepByStepInstructions.instruction: Click Develop on the context toolbar. The processed image opens in Pixel Studio; the original RAW file remains unaltered.

visualExamples.title: Color Bit Depth Pipeline Comparison
visualExamples.description: Why 32-bit float and 16-bit matter for professional colorists.
visualExamples.visualContent:
| Bit Depth | Total Discrete Tonal Levels per Channel | Dynamic Range Behavior | Primary Usage |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8-bit Integer | 256 levels (0-255) | Clamps at 0 (black) and 255 (white); banding risk | Web JPEG, final export |
| 16-bit Integer | 65,536 levels | Smooth gradients; zero posterization during grading | Professional retouching |
| 32-bit Float | Billions of values (unbounded) | Values can exceed 1.0; true HDR physical light data | VFX, 3D render comps, RAW |

visualExamples.title: Bayer Sensor De-Mosaicing Diagram
visualExamples.description: How the Develop Studio reconstructs full color from RAW sensor data.
visualExamples.visualContent:
Camera CMOS Sensor [RG/GB Bayer Pattern]
   ↓ Raw Sensor Voltage
Develop Studio [De-mosaicing Algorithm]
   ├── White Balance Matrix Calibration
   ├── Unbounded Highlight/Shadow Recovery
   └── Lens Distortion & Vignette Correction
   ↓
Photo Persona [Full 16-bit or 32-bit Pixel Canvas]

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Over-pushing Shadows causing heavy digital noise
commonPitfalls.cause: Under-exposed shadow areas contain low signal-to-noise ratio; pushing the Shadows slider to +100% amplifies raw sensor read noise.
commonPitfalls.solution: Balance shadow recovery with the Noise Reduction slider in the 'Details' panel, applying Color Noise reduction to tame chroma speckles.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Developing directly into 8-bit and discarding color headroom
commonPitfalls.cause: If the Output setting is set to 8-bit, 98% of the camera sensor's original tonal gradation is permanently discarded upon clicking Develop.
commonPitfalls.solution: Always verify that Output is set to 'RGB (16-bit)' or 'RGB (32-bit)' in the Develop Studio top context bar.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: Unintentional color shifting when moving between computers
commonPitfalls.cause: Mismatch between camera sensor profile (Adobe RGB / ProPhoto) and monitor sRGB space.
commonPitfalls.solution: Enable Soft Proofing adjustment in Photo Persona to preview target destination color gamut.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary benefit of developing a RAW file into a 32-bit floating-point workspace (RGB/32 HDR)?
options: It makes the image file size smaller than a JPEG.
It permits unbounded luminance values where highlights can exceed 1.0 (pure white), allowing subsequent adjustments to recover blown details that would be permanently clipped in 8-bit or 16-bit.
It forces the camera to take another picture.
It converts the image into vector paths.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: 32-bit floating point color representation is unbounded. Values above 1.0 represent real physical light values, allowing retouchers to dim intense highlights later without experiencing white clipping.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which panel is documented for manual lens distortion and chromatic-aberration corrections in Develop Studio?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The current Affinity RAW guide assigns distortion, rotation, chromatic aberration, defringing and vignetting corrections to the Lens panel.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does checking 'Remove Chromatic Aberration' in the Lens tab accomplish?
options: It deletes all green colors from the photo.
It detects and removes optical color fringing (typically magenta/purple and green halos) caused by light wavelengths refracting at slightly different angles through camera lens elements.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Chromatic aberration is an optical artifact where colors fail to converge at the same focal point. Affinity Photo's algorithm detects and neutralizes these peripheral color fringes.

summaryPoints: Develop Studio opens supported RAW files automatically for non-destructive processing.
Basic, Lens, Detail, Tones and Masks panels organize the documented RAW workflow.
Output can be a Pixel layer, an embedded RAW layer or a linked RAW layer.
The Develop command sends the processed image to Pixel Studio.

slides.title: RAW Develop Studio & 32-bit HDR Pipelines
slides.subtitle: Unleashing the Full Power of Digital Camera Sensors
slides.contentMarkdown: When you open a supported RAW file, Affinity automatically launches **Develop Studio**, a dedicated environment for RAW processing. This lesson covers exposure, white balance, lens correction, detail refinement and the available output modes.

actionBox.label: The RAW Advantage
actionBox.text: RAW files contain up to 14 stops of dynamic range—twice the dynamic range of an 8-bit JPEG.

slides.title: Bit Depth & The 32-bit Floating Point Revolution
slides.subtitle: Why Integers Limit You and Floats Set You Free
slides.contentMarkdown:
Traditional image editors lock your artwork into **8-bit integers (0 to 255)**:
- If a cloud hits 255, it's clipped to pure white forever. Darkening it later only produces muddy gray.

**Affinity Photo's 32-bit Float (RGB/32 HDR)** is completely **unbounded**:
- Bright sunlight or light bulbs can register as `2.5` or `10.0`.
- You can darken the sky three stops later in Photo Persona, and the cloud texture miraculously reappears!

visual.content: 8-bit (256 steps, clamped) vs 16-bit (65,536 steps) vs 32-bit Float (Billions of values, unbounded HDR)

slides.title: Develop Studio panels
slides.subtitle: Basic, Lens & Details Panels
slides.contentMarkdown:
The current RAW workflow organizes its controls into panels:

- **Basic:** exposure, black point, brightness, tone curve, enhance, white balance, shadows and highlights.
- **Lens:** distortion, rotation, chromatic aberration, defringing and vignetting.
- **Detail:** noise reduction and sharpening.
- **Tones:** tonal curves, black-and-white conversion and split toning.
- **Masks:** selective brush or gradient masks.

actionBox.label: Clipping Shortcut
actionBox.text: Start with Basic, then use Lens and Detail panels where the source image requires them.

slides.title: Step-by-Step: RAW Sky & Shadow Recovery
slides.subtitle: A Practical Colorist Workflow
slides.contentMarkdown:
1. **Open RAW:** Open a supported RAW file. It launches Develop Studio automatically.
2. **Basic corrections:** Adjust Exposure, Highlights, Shadows, Temperature and Tint in the Basic panel.
3. **Lens corrections:** Use the Lens panel for distortion and chromatic aberration where applicable.
4. **Detail refinement:** Review noise reduction and sharpening in the Detail panel.
5. **Output:** Choose Pixel layer, RAW layer (embedded) or RAW layer (linked), then click Develop to enter Pixel Studio.

visual.content: Always develop into 16-bit or 32-bit Output to retain pristine color fidelity during final grading.

slides.title: RAW Development Pitfalls & Fixes
slides.subtitle: Preventing Noise and Color Banding
slides.contentMarkdown:
### 1. Over-adjusting shadows
- **Risk:** Strong shadow lifting can reveal sensor noise.
- **Approach:** Review noise in the Detail panel and apply measured noise reduction.

### 2. Choosing an output type
- **Pixel layer:** developed pixel result.
- **RAW layer (embedded):** the RAW source is copied into the document.
- **RAW layer (linked):** the RAW source remains in its original location.

### 3. Applying unnecessary corrections
- Use the Lens and Detail panels only where the image/source file calls for them.

actionBox.label: Pro-Tip
actionBox.text: RAW noise is easiest to tame before demosaicing artifacts are baked in.

slides.subtitle: Perfecting High-Contrast Architecture
slides.contentMarkdown:
### Your Mission:
Develop a supported RAW architectural photograph:
1. Correct white balance using a neutral area.
2. Use Lens-panel controls to reduce distortion and chromatic aberration where available.
3. Review Detail-panel noise reduction and sharpening.
4. Choose an output mode and develop the image into Pixel Studio.

### Acceptance Criteria:
- White balance is visually neutral.
- Applicable lens corrections improve straight edges and color fringing.
- Detail refinement preserves texture.
- The original RAW source remains available when an embedded or linked RAW output is chosen.
